/cards/10/segments/0/text: When the mistress remained in bed for days, the servants lent rooms to their relations and took whatever they wanted from the house. Sometimes there was no need even to conceal it. The only person who truly saw what they were doing was a girl in an orphanage uniform.
/cards/10/segments/1/text: [[NPC1]] refused to pretend she had seen nothing. So she endured torments that were difficult to name as serious offences: doors locked her in, errands were deliberately complicated. She had to watch for missing possessions while fearing that her mistress would accuse her of taking them. The servants knew the house better than she did. They also knew how far a child without a family to defend her could be pushed.
/cards/10/segments/2/text: Occasionally {{e_maria|María}} emerged from her preoccupations and talked to her, revealing wit, insight and warmth. Just as the girl began to feel attached to her, the next day's gaze would pass over her as if she were a familiar piece of furniture. The lady need not lose her temper to spend an entire day without really seeing her.
/cards/10/segments/3/text: She remembered the duties {{e_abbess|Mother Pilar}} had given her. She had been sent as a companion, with no promise that she would be happy. When unhappiness came, she first wondered whether she had done her duty properly. Soft footsteps, quietly closed doors, coming at once when called: all these were easier than explaining why she was hurt.
/cards/10/segments/4/text: The great house had room for the servants' relations, chests of presents and portraits of the daughter overseas. After moving in, the girl still could find no one to whom she could safely speak. She finished her work and waited for another day when her mistress might care to talk. She still wore her convent uniform. Her mistress had not thought to provide another dress.
/cards/11/segments/0/text: {{e_maria|María}} told me to stay in the sunshine. She would not be long. This stone is still warm, but now the shadow has reached my shoes. I thought of going into the church to look for her. What if she came out and could not find me?
/cards/11/segments/1/text: At last I went in. She was not there. I searched the pews, reached another door, and understood that she had probably left by it. May I go home now? Or must I return to the place where she told me to wait? Her instruction was so simple. I have made it harder and harder.
/cards/11/segments/2/text: People are always passing through the square in {{e_lima|Lima}}. When I hear lowered voices, I think they are talking about my clothes. Perhaps some have not even looked at me, but I still want to hide the edge of my skirt. Everyone knows this uniform. Everyone knows where I came from.
/cards/11/segments/3/text: {{e_obedience|Obedience}} ought to make things clear. Do as you are told and you will disappoint no one. I return to the same corner and stand in the lengthening shadow. If she passes this way once more, she will know that I did not wander off.
/cards/12/segments/0/text: During the interval, [[NPC2]] set aside her dignified role and came before the curtain to sing the topical songs popular in the city. She had noticed the old lady in her box. She improvised verses about her looks, her drinking, her stinginess, even her daughter's departure overseas. {{e_pio|Pio}} ordinarily helped her learn her lines and judge a performance. These improvised songs were hers to control.
/cards/12/segments/1/text: The audience understood quickly. Eyes turned from the stage to the box, and laughter rose in successive waves. [[NPC1]] was still thinking of the two acts she had just seen, and of {{e_spain|Spain}}. Her attention had wandered far away. A few fine phrases were forming in her mind; perhaps her daughter would like them in a letter.
/cards/12/segments/2/text: The singer grew bolder. Beside the lady, [[NPC3]] heard everything. She tugged her sleeve and quietly urged her to leave. She did not rise to argue with the whole theatre; she only wanted to take her mistress beyond those staring eyes. When the two left the box, the audience rose cheering, as though a battle had been won.
/cards/12/segments/3/text: The actress broke into a lively dance. Seeing the manager behind the stage, she knew that this triumph would increase her fee. The audience's {{e_applause|Applause}} assured her that today's cruelty had succeeded.
/cards/12/segments/4/text: The old lady being led outside was almost pleased. The performance had given her phrases that might amuse her daughter. She did not know that she too had become material for someone else's amusement. In the same uproar, the actress heard approval, the girl heard humiliation, and the lady heard almost nothing. Everyone had looked towards her box. No one had waited for her answer.
/cards/13/segments/0/text: The actress arrived in black, carrying a letter from {{e_viceroy|Viceroy Andrés}}. [[NPC1]] rubbed her forehead with snow, put on her cloak and struggled into the drawing room. [[NPC2]] had prepared a few perfunctory remarks. Now the old lady's bearing unsettled her.
/cards/13/segments/1/text: You have come—was there something you wished?
/cards/13/segments/2/text: I wanted to be certain that you had not misunderstood what you heard at the theatre that evening. An actress such as myself sometimes says more than she means.
/cards/13/segments/3/text: Misunderstood? I remember only how beautifully you acted. You are a great artist. You ought to be happy.
/cards/13/segments/4/text: I mean the songs between the acts. I feared you might think I had intended to show you disrespect.
/cards/13/segments/5/text: Ah, we left early. Forgive us—right in the middle of your wonderful performance. I forget why. Someone was unwell, perhaps.
/cards/13/segments/6/text: The actress blushed. She could not believe that anyone had failed to understand the songs. She could only interpret these words as forgiveness.
/cards/13/segments/7/text: You are so good, to forgive my childishness. I did not know before. Please let me kiss your hand.
/cards/13/segments/8/text: How could I be angry with you, my beautiful child? One of your gestures reminded me of {{e_clara|Clara}}. Once we quarrelled, then both returned to ask forgiveness, with only a door between us. She took my face in both hands, like this.
/cards/13/segments/9/text: Weeping, the lady leaned forward to demonstrate the gesture she had dreamed so often. That reconciliation had never occurred in her waking life.
/cards/13/segments/10/text: People in the city say she treats me badly. It is not true. She is intelligent and gracious; I am the difficult one. I weary people when I speak, and yet I became the mother of so beautiful a girl.
/cards/13/segments/11/text: She almost fell from the chair. {{e_pepita|Pepita}} steadied her and took her back to her room. At home, the actress stood a long while before her mirror, both hands against her own face. She had not brought back the easy relief she had expected from the apology.
/cards/14/segments/0/text: The news was almost hidden at the end of the letter. {{e_clara|Clara}} wrote that she could not travel that autumn as planned: her child would be born in early October. She made little of it, hoping to provoke less anxiety in her mother. [[NPC1]] caught hold of the wall. What child? Her daughter was to become a mother?
/cards/14/segments/1/text: She began asking questions at once. What did the old women of the city know? Which remedies were said to work? She gathered everything and put it into letters. Details that bored the reader across the sea became her most urgent daily business. The greater the distance and the less she could do, the more she wanted to try every possibility.
/cards/14/segments/2/text: There must be no knots in the house; even the maids could not tie their hair tightly. She marked the even-numbered stairs with red chalk. When someone stepped wrongly she wept, shouted and drove them out. She concealed protective charms on her body, as though one oversight might harm the life about to begin across the sea.
/cards/14/segments/3/text: Before daybreak she went to the earliest Mass. Gripping the altar rail, she gazed at the sacred images and begged for the slightest nod. Yet after a day of such exertion she sometimes felt that nature was deaf and God indifferent. Nothing she did had touched the course of events.
/cards/14/segments/4/text: The despair never lasted. As soon as a new 'perhaps' arose, she hurried home to replace the candles. At last she decided to make a pilgrimage to the {{e_shrine|Shrine of Cluxambuqua}}. Her chair would cross the {{e_bridge|Bridge of San Luis Rey}} and climb into the Andes. She hoped the ancient shrine might offer a firmer assurance than the markings in her house. She performed every observance earnestly, with ever less certainty that she could still protect her daughter.
/cards/15/segments/0/text: {{e_maria|María}} went straight to the shrine without getting out of her chair at the door. She has left this place to me. By the time she returns, it must at least be a room one can live in. The porters are waiting. I show them which basket goes by the wall and which must be opened first.
/cards/15/segments/1/text: The altar, tapestries and portraits of her daughter all have to come out. This room at the {{e_inn|Mountain Inn}} is not the room at home. If the arrangement feels strange, she may be unable to settle. It is cold here; the brazier must be prepared. I must go downstairs and tell the cook how to make the {{e_porridge|Porridge}}. I cannot be vague about that. It is mostly what she manages to eat.
/cards/15/segments/2/text: The mountain air makes me dizzy. I press my hand against the table and wait for it to pass, thinking of what remains undone. As long as I do one thing after another, there is no time to think how far away the {{e_convent|Saint Rose's Convent}} has become.
/cards/15/segments/3/text: At last the room is ready, but there are still no footsteps outside. With nothing to do, familiar voices return: advice at supper, prayers beside the sickbeds, the abbess asking me to stay and talk. I take out paper, then lay down the quill. A letter should not delay my work very much. At least there will be hot porridge to her liking when she comes back.
/cards/16/segments/0/text: When the white-walled mountain town came into view, [[NPC1]]'s fingers stopped moving over her rosary. The Andes rose so high that the town seemed to rest upon their knees. Bells answered one another. In the clear cold air her hurried prayers suddenly ceased to tumble out in succession.
/cards/16/segments/1/text: At the shrine an attendant demanded an obscure fee, then asked her to move on the pretext of repairing the floor. Elsewhere this might have disturbed her. Today she changed places and remained seated. The old candle-sellers talked of money all day; even they did not interrupt her. Dimly she felt that perhaps her daughter's life and the affairs of God did not need her constant urging.
/cards/16/segments/2/text: Later she sat beside the fountain, watching the sick move slowly around the garden and three hawks circle above. A thick-fleeced llama approached, bringing its soft nose near as though it too wished to join a conversation. Others followed, gathering round this woman who was no longer in a hurry.
/cards/16/segments/3/text: A messenger boy found her. She had ordered that any news from {{e_spain|Spain}} be brought immediately. She opened the packet, first reading her son-in-law's witty, affectionate note, then {{e_clara|Clara}}'s letter. Her daughter's clever sentences had sharp edges. As each one wounded her, she wrapped it in understanding and forgiveness and laid it in her heart.
/cards/16/segments/4/text: This time she did not rush away or send anyone on an errand. She put away the {{e_letters|Letters}}, rose slowly, gently dispersed the curious llamas and returned to the shrine. The square's bells were still ringing. Her face was grave, but she no longer asked the world what more she must do to obtain assurance. She did not tell the strangers nearby of her daughter's harshness. She kept the letter in her own hands.
/cards/17/title: May I Come Back for a Few Days?
/cards/17/segments/0/text: I only meant to tell {{e_abbess|Mother Pilar}} that we had safely reached the {{e_inn|Mountain Inn}}. Yet the ink spots kept multiplying as I wrote. She is so busy. Will seeing them make her worry about me too?
/cards/17/segments/1/text: …None of it matters, so long as you love me and wish me to stay with the lady. I ought not to tell you, but sometimes the wicked maids lock me in my room and take things away. Perhaps the lady will think I have stolen them. I hope not. I hope you are well, and that there is no trouble at the hospital or anywhere else.
/cards/17/segments/2/text: Though I cannot see you, I think of you all the time and remember what you have taught me. I only want to do what you wish. But might I come back to the convent for a few days? If you do not wish it, there is no need. I am only so lonely, with no one to talk to, and other things…
/cards/17/segments/3/text: Sometimes I do not know whether you have forgotten me. If you could find a little time to write even a very short letter, I could keep it with me. But I know how busy you are…
/cards/17/segments/4/text: She put down the quill and left the ink-spotted letter. Downstairs she asked about fresh {{e_charcoal|Charcoal}} and tasted the porridge in the pot. Among these small tasks, her hands once more knew exactly what to do.
/cards/18/segments/0/text: [[NPC1]] had read the girl's letter on the table. After closing it, she wanted to read it again. She envied the devotion that {{e_abbess|Mother Pilar}} inspired in a child, and felt ashamed of making love so burdensome herself. The girl brought in supper.
/cards/18/segments/1/text: Child, will you not eat with me?
/cards/18/segments/2/text: I thought you would be tired. I have eaten downstairs. Shall I read to you while you eat?
/cards/18/segments/3/text: No, thank you. Go to bed if you wish. Wait—I am sending a letter to Lima tomorrow morning. If you have one, it can go with mine.
/cards/18/segments/4/text: I have none. I must go down and fetch fresh charcoal for you.
/cards/18/segments/5/text: But the one to the abbess… I know she would be delighted to receive it.
/cards/18/segments/6/text: I am not sending it. I have changed my mind. It was not a good letter.
/cards/18/segments/7/text: Why not, my dear? I thought it very beautiful. Believe me, I know about such things. What made it a bad letter?
/cards/18/segments/9/text: The girl would say no more. She took the letter into her room. The woman at the table heard paper tearing and looked down at her supper. {{e_courage|Courage}}: she had never seriously brought that word into love. Remembering her demands for answers, she first wanted to defend herself, to blame her upbringing and circumstances. At last she cleared the table and sat down to write again.
/cards/18/segments/10/text: This became the fifty-sixth of her celebrated {{e_letters|Letters}}. She called it her first, as though her appeals could finally take another form. She could not retrieve the old letters that repeatedly asked how much her daughter loved her. This new one could still be more generous. When she finished, dawn was near.
/cards/19/segments/0/text: Once I said that word, I wanted to say nothing more. {{e_maria|María}} kept looking at me. She really thought the letter beautiful. I am not used to anyone asking why I will not send it.
/cards/19/segments/1/text: Tearing paper makes a loud sound. In such a quiet room at the {{e_inn|Mountain Inn}}, it must be audible next door. I tore it smaller, but the things I had written did not disappear. I still want to go back for a few days. I still wish {{e_abbess|Mother Pilar}} would write me a few words, even a letter small enough to fit in my palm.
/cards/19/segments/2/text: After lying down I remember how I spoke, and feel uneasy. I should not have spoken so loudly. Perhaps I should not have called it a bad letter. Now the paper is in pieces, and asking for another sheet would mean explaining everything again. No one questions me in the dark. I am still answering in my head.
/cards/19/segments/3/text: Eventually the girl slept. Near dawn, the lady came in holding a candle and gently brushed the damp hair from her forehead. The unsent letter never returned to the mailbag. Two days later they set out for the city, towards the {{e_bridge|Bridge of San Luis Rey}} they had crossed on their way there.
